entries.title: Bulls coaching vacancy living up to the promise of casting a wide net
entries.summary: <p>Recently hired executive vice president of basketball operations Bryson Graham made it sound like a wide net would be used for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls’</a> coaching search and that is proving to be the case.</p><p>The team has already been rumored to have a list of up-and-comers like San Antonio assistant Sean Sweeney, Minnesota’s Micah Nori, Oklahoma City’s Dave Bliss, former player Jerry Stackhouse, and even an in-house candidate in assistant Wes Unseld Jr. on the radar.</p><p>Miami assistant Chris Quinn is now in the mix, as the Bulls have reportedly received permission to talk to Quinn about the vacancy left when Billy Donovan opted to walk away from the head coaching seat after six seasons.</p><p>Quinn fits the job description that Graham laid out when he was hired, not only having a strong reputation for player development, but it doesn’t hurt that he’s worked under Erik Spoelstra — arguably one of the elite coaches in the league — since 2014.</p><p>Again, this remains a process for Graham, who may have to play the long game in a coaching hire with Bliss and Sweeney still involved in the Western Conference Finals.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Teen sets Kane County Cougars' bus ablaze in Winnipeg
entries.summary: <p>The Kane County Cougars’ bus was set on fire and destroyed early Thursday in Winnipeg, Manitoba, and a 15-year-old girl is facing charges related to arson. No one was hurt.</p><p>The Cougars, who were in town to play the Goldeyes in the American Association of Professional Baseball, were in their hotel when the teen allegedly set fire to the bus, which was engulfed in flames. Police arrived at the scene at around 1:50 a.m., and firefighters extinguished the blaze.</p><p>"Everyone is OK, and we are still determining if any gear or personal property was lost," Cougars vice president and general manager Curtis Haug told CBC News.</p><p>The Goldeyes helped the Cougars procure a bus to take them to Fargo, North Dakota, the next stop on their road trip. Windstar, the company whose bus was destroyed, will send a bus to Fargo to bring the Geneva-based Cougars home.</p><p>"We are very disappointed that this could happen to our family-owned company, and the loss of this vehicle will impact our business and operations," Windstar operations manager Jackson Greteman wrote in an email to CBC News, adding that the bus was worth $425,000.</p><p>"We are happy that no one was hurt in this reckless act of vandalism and are cooperating with local authorities."</p><p>Police at first took two teens into custody. The girl facing charges was released.<br></p>

entries.title: St. Patrick football star David Folorunsho commits to Notre Dame
entries.summary: <p>David Folorunsho grew up playing soccer in Nigeria.</p><p>Now he’s a centerpiece of Notre Dame football’s 2027 recruiting class.</p><p>It has been quite a journey for the St. Patrick junior.</p><p>“I’m blessed to be in this situation,” Folorunsho told the Sun-Time after announcing his commitment to Notre Dame on May 15 in a ceremony at St. Patrick. “I can’t put anything on me. I got to put it to Jesus Christ.”</p><p>A 6-3, 280-pound defensive lineman, Folorunsho is the consensus No. 2 player in Illinois in the 2027 cycle, the No. 3 defensive lineman nationally and the No. 43 player overall.</p><p>He moved from Nigeria to the United States when he was 11 and kept playing soccer for a few years. Then some friends invited him to football practice, and his athletic path was set.</p><p>He played offensive line before moving to the other side of the ball, a switch that suited him well.</p><p>What does he like about his current position?</p><p>“Just attacking, getting after the quarterback,” Folorunsho said. “I like to use my athleticism; that’s the main reason.”</p><p>Colleges have taken notice.</p><p>Folorunsho has more than 30 Power Four offers, including from Indiana, Ohio State, Alabama, Georgia, LSU, Miami, Michigan and Texas.</p><p>“David is a player with an unlimited upside,” national recruiting analyst Clint Cosgrove said. “He’s got a lot of physical talent. He’s still raw at this point, but as well as he’s still growing into his body, there’s a lot to like about him.</p><p>“He fires off the ball. . . . He’s a high, high motor kid.”</p><p>St. Patrick coach Tom Zbikowski, an All-America defensive back at Notre Dame before moving on to the NFL, said he didn’t steer Folorunsho to his alma mater.</p><p>“I kept it neutral,” Zbikowski told the Sun-Times. “I wanted him to do his own studying, take a real good look at all those programs. They’re all good programs — you’re not going to make a bad decision out of there.”</p><p>At the end of the process, though, Zbikowski said, “I think family . . . and him understanding that once football’s over that this is the best option for him and it can do the most for you, especially being from Chicago.</p><p>“It’s a different animal when you’re a Chicago kid that goes to Notre Dame.”</p><p>Academics were a major component of Folorunsho’s decision.</p><p>“I want to go for business marketing, and they have a great business school and great contacts to help me out with that,” he said.</p><p>Now Folorunsho can focus on his final season with the Shamrocks, who were 6-5 in Zbikowski’s first year.</p><p>“The main thing I’m going to emphasize is pad level and really shoot my hands, getting that knock-back [of] an O-lineman,” he said. “More pass-rush moves and just being more consistent with every rep.”</p><p>“He works every day in the morning, and he works every day after school,” Zbikowski said. “I think he loves the process of getting better every day.</p><p>“He loves football — really loves football. I know a lot of people play football, and they all want to be D1 until it’s time to be D1 and understand all that goes into it. I don’t think he’s going to shy away from that. In fact, I think that’s what’s going to bring the best out of him.<br></p>

entries.title: Northwestern women's lacrosse team beats Johns Hopkins to return to NCAA title game
entries.summary: <p>Madison Taylor and Maddie Epke scored four goals apiece, and Northwestern’s women’s lacrosse team beat Johns Hopkins 16-11 in the national semifinals Friday in Evanston to return to the NCAA championship game. The Wildcats will face North Carolina, which beat Maryland 16-6 in the first semifinal, at 11 a.m. Sunday at Martin Stadium.</p><p>Northwestern (17-3), the first school to host the women’s lacrosse championship outside the Eastern Time Zone, lost to the Tar Heels in the national final last year 12-8. The Cats are looking for their first national title since 2023 and ninth under coach Kelly Amonte Hiller.</p><p>Aditi Foster scored three goals, and Taylor Lapointe and Kate Ratanaproeksa had two each for the Wildcats, who outshot the Blue Jays 40-22. Ava Angello led the Blue Jays (17-4) with three goals.</p><p>Northwestern trailed 1-0, tied the score almost two minutes later and never trailed again. The Wildcats led 10-3 at halftime before the Blue Jays cut the deficit to three late in the third quarter. After Epke and Lapointe scored about a minute apart, the Blue Jays never got closer than within four again.<br></p>

entries.title: Rookie reliever Tyler Davis earning trust in White Sox' bullpen
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a> have had a line of relievers racking up frequent-flyer miles between Chicago and Triple-A Charlotte, but <b>Tyler Davis’</b> spot on the big-league charter should be secure if he keeps throwing the ball like he has over his first month in the majors.</p><p>Davis, who was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/23/white-sox-bryan-hudson-munetaka-murakami-tyler-davis" target="_blank" ><u>solely a position player</u></a> in his final college season and just started focusing exclusively on throwing a couple of years ago, contributed another shutdown inning in a combined Sox <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/19/white-sox-mariners-rally-meidroth-benintendi?55" target="_blank" ><u>one-hitter</u></a> Tuesday in Seattle. He arrived in San Francisco with a 3.09 ERA in 10 outings, nine of which were hitless, with eight walks and 11 strikeouts.</p><p>“He’s very competitive,” manager <b>Will Venable</b> said. “He’s got good stuff, and he’s not afraid to throw it in the zone. He’s a guy that really quickly earned trust here.”</p><p>Batters were hitting .091 against his fastball, which averages 96 mph.</p><p>“Just trusting myself, just trusting my ability and trusting what the catcher puts down and then having conviction in what I throw,” Davis said.</p><h3>Noah walking a fine line</h3><p>Rookie left-hander <b>Noah Schultz’s</b> start Monday against the Mariners marked his first big-league outing without issuing a walk.</p><p>“I did hit two guys, but no walks is definitely a step in the right direction,” Schultz said.</p><p>The walks had been the biggest problem over what has otherwise been a mostly promising rookie campaign for the Sox’ top pitching prospect, at 2-3 with a 4.93 ERA in seven starts (34⅔ innings) with 21 walks and 32 strikeouts.</p><p>Schultz, who’s scheduled to start Sunday against the Giants, said his latest focus is on “my posture. Making myself go straight to the plate, not doing too much being over-rotational.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a Sox have turned around early this season, slashing .240/.397/.560 in 50 pinch-hitting at-bats. Sox pinch hitters went an anemic .134/.216/.157 last season without a homer.</p><p>“I love it,” Hills said of his late-game opportunities. “It’s an absolute blessing to be even considered to go up there and execute in that position, so I don’t take it lightly.”</p><h3>Injuries in the outfield</h3><p>Left fielder <b>Austin Hays</b> (calf strain) progressed well through his first three games of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/04/white-sox-sign-outfielder-randal-grichuk-put-outfielder-austin-hays-on-injured-list" target="_blank" ><u>a rehab assignment</u></a> this week at Charlotte and will be reevaluated after playing another series this weekend, Venable said.</p><p>The timetable is less clear for outfielder <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/21/everson-pereira-white-sox-outfield" target="_blank" ><b><u>Everson Pereira</u></b></a>, who is swinging but hasn’t thrown at full speed since a shoulder injury landed him on the injured list April 29. “I didn’t expect this to linger for this long,” Pereira said through interpreter <b>Billy Russo</b>.</p><p>It all leaves outfield roster questions, with <b>Sam Antonacci</b> entrenching himself in left and <b>Tristan Peters</b> holding down in center.</p><p>“We’ve still got a few days before Austin comes back, and we’ll see what happens between then and now,” Venable said. “Really good problems to have, when you have a lot of guys on your roster that are doing a really good job on a daily basis.”</p><p><b>Jarred Kelenic</b>, who has logged regular playing time in right field this month, was a late scratch Friday after getting hit in the lower back by a ball during the Giants’ batting practice. entries.title: Dr. Olusimbo Ige out as Chicago health chief
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Department of Public Health Commissioner Dr. Olusimbo Ige has resigned from her position, the mayor’s office confirmed Friday.</p><p>Fikirte Wagaw, the CDPH first deputy commissioner, will serve as acting commissioner, according to a spokesperson for Mayor Brandon Johnson’s office, who added that the mayor “will work expeditiously to identify a permanent replacement.”</p><p>A source familiar with the matter confirmed Friday that Johnson had asked for Ige's resignation, which is effective immediately.</p><p>“Today, Mayor Johnson accepted Dr. Ige’s letter of resignation. We thank her for her expertise and years of service as Commissioner for the Chicago Department of Public Health (CDPH),” a spokesperson for the mayor’s office said in a statement.</p><p>Ige is a public health expert — trained in medicine in Nigeria, where she grew up, and not licensed to practice in the U.S. Before taking the Chicago job, she worked for the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. Before that, she served as an assistant commissioner at New York City’s health department.</p><p>Johnson chose her from among four finalists produced by a nationwide search led by a committee that included former Illinois Department of Public Health Director Dr. Ngozi Ezike; Dr. Wayne H. Giles, dean of the School of Public Health at the University of Illinois at Chicago; Dr. David Ansell, a high-ranking official at Rush University Medical Center; and Arturo Carrillo, who at the time was deputy director for health and violence prevention at the Brighton Park Neighborhood Council.</p><p>Carrillo is now the city's deputy mayor for health and human services. Reached by the Sun-Times Friday evening, he had no comment on Ige's departure. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2023/11/13/23958969/mayor-brandon-johnson-chooses-chicago-health-commissioner-olusimbo-ige-replace-allison-arwady" target="_blank" >Ige was announced</a> as public health commissioner by Johnson in November 2023 just months after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/8/11/23827860/chicago-public-health-chief-dr-allison-arwady-brandon-johnson-lightfoot" target="_blank" >the mayor fired Dr. Allison Arwady</a>, a pediatrician and infectious diseases expert who led the city through the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/coronavirus" target="_blank" >COVID-19 pandemic</a>.</p><p>Arwady also had clashed with the Chicago Teachers Union for opening Chicago Public Schools during the pandemic earlier than the union wanted them to open without the protections the CTU had demanded.</p><p>Arwady's firing came as no surprise. Johnson was a paid organizer of the CTU who owed his election to the millions of dollars contributed by the union and the hundreds of foot soldiers the group and its affiliates provided.</p><p>Like Ige, Arwady was fired late on a Friday.<br></p>

entries.title: White Sox' nine-run inning outweighs rare shaky start from Davis Martin for win over Giants
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO — The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" ><u>White Sox</u></a>’ biggest inning of offense in three years made up for one of ace Davis Martin’s only uneven starts of the season en route to a 9-4 victory Friday night to open their three-game set against the Giants.</p><p>The Sox went hitless outside their fourth-inning outburst, which came without any home runs — another rarity for this season's homer-happy squad. </p><p>"It's a little different for us, but that's what the offense can do," said Martin, whose ERA rose to a still-stellar 2.04, third-lowest in the American League. "We can win and do different things."</p><p>Giants starter Trevor McDonald mowed down the Sox’ first run through the order but unraveled as he hit Sam Antonacci and Munetaka Murakami with pitches to open the fourth. A Colson Montgomery single, a Chase Meidroth walk and an Andrew Benintendi double later, and the Sox had three on the board.</p><p>The nightmare inning for San Fran dragged on with a run-scoring fielder’s choice by Edgar Quero and an RBI single for Derek Hill before Antonacci got hit again in the same inning by Giants reliever and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/02/13/ryan-borucki-white-sox-fan-bullpen-spring-training" target="_blank" ><u>Mundelein native</u></a> Ryan Borucki to load the bases. Murakami cleared them with a double to the left-field corner to make it 8-0.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">what a 4th inning! 👏 <a href="https://t.co/zIzjp28yph">pic.twitter.com/zIzjp28yph</a></p>— Chicago White Sox (@whitesox) <a href="https://twitter.com/whitesox/status/2058027080705622141?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">May 23, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.twitter.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The Giants looked like they were finally about to escape the inning on Miguel Vargas’ grounder, but shortstop Willy Adames’ throw sailed down the first-base line to score Murakami. Borucki finally struck out Montgomery to end the inning, drawing sarcastic applause at Oracle Park.</p><p>The nine-spot marked the most the Sox had scored in an inning since their 11-run outburst against the Reds on May 7, 2023.</p><p>Antonacci’s double-plunking in a single inning was a franchise first, according to the team, and not since former Cub John Lackey hit Jose Abreu, Matt Davidson and Yoan Moncada in the fifth inning of their July 25, 2017, Crosstown matchup had three Sox been beaned in a frame.</p><p>"Sounds fitting for Sam," manager Will Venable said. "That’s part of his game, which is rare for guys... He stands in there, doesn’t get out of the way sometimes. So credit for him for standing in there."</p><p>The Giants loaded the bases against Martin in the fifth, plating two as Adames grounded into a forceout and Luis Arraez knocked an infield single through the left side. After a wild pitch from Martin, San Francisco left fielder Casey Schmitt’s groundout added another to make it 9-3.</p><p>Matt Chapman doubled off Martin to open San Francisco’s half of the sixth and came around on catcher Jesus Rodriguez’s groundout. When Montgomery fumbled a grounder that would’ve ended the inning, manager Will Venable called it a night for Martin at 5 ⅔ innings with four runs on six hits and two walks with seven strikeouts.</p><p>It was just the second start of 10 in Martin’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/04/29/davis-martin-white-sox-breakout-season" target="_blank" ><u>breakout season</u></a> that he’s given up more than two runs, ending a six-start streak of one-run or shutout outings. He gave up three runs over five innings in his first outing of the year in Miami. </p><p>Relievers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/05/22/tyler-davis-white-sox-noah-schultz" target="_blank" ><u>Tyler Davis</u></a>, Brandon Eisert and Trevor Richards did the rest.</p><p>"It's always good to have a bad day when your offense scores nine," Davis said.</p>

Why not? “Eat, drink and be merry!”</p><h2>Aquarius (Jan. 20-Feb. 18)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-4d0000" name="html-embed-module-4d0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>An <b>average</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> In discussions about wills, inheritances, taxes, debt, or shared property, you'll have no trouble standing your ground. You feel confident and determined. Fortunately, you are also charming and fun-loving. (You will get what you want.)</p><h2>Pisces (Feb. 19-March 20)</h2> <p></p> <div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-7b0000" name="html-embed-module-7b0000"></a><div class="HoroscopeStarbox HoroscopeStarbox_five"> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_container"> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> <svg class="HoroscopeStar"><use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use></svg> </div> <div class="HoroscopeStarbox_description"> <p>A <b>positive</b> day</p> </div> </div> <style> .HoroscopeStarbox { background: #f8f8f8; display: flex; align-items: center; } .HoroscopeStarbox_container { display: grid; grid-gap: 5px; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr 1fr; padding: 20px; width: 40%; min-width: 160px; max-width: 200px; } .HoroscopeStarbox_description { padding: 20px; font-family: var(--font-1); font-size: var(--body-2); } .HoroscopeStarbox_container svg { object-fit: cover; aspect-ratio: 1 / 1; width: 100%; } </style> </div> </div><p> You might attract someone to you today who is enthusiastic. Or perhaps you will be the enthusiastic person who bowls somebody else over. Either way, discussions at home about repairs and family matters will be lively.</p><h2>If today is your birthday</h2><p>Actress Joan Collins (1933) shares your birthday today. You're vibrant, enthusiastic and charming. You're constantly curious about life's mysteries. This is a slower-paced year. Take time to rejuvenate your energy. Focus on business and personal relationships with people who are kind, helpful and have your back. Concentrate on your needs and what brings you happiness.</p>

entries.title: America's shameful retreat from racial reckoning, 6 years after George Floyd's murder
entries.summary: <p>Six years ago, the murder of George Floyd forced a national and long-overdue racial reckoning, drawing millions of Americans into the streets to demand justice for generations of Black Americans facing systemic racism. </p><p>For a moment, it seemed possible that America was prepared to engage honestly with our history and commit to meaningful systemic change. </p><p>Today, however, that awakening faces a fierce, organized backlash — a coordinated attempt to distort our history, roll back civil rights protections and hand down legal decisions that ignore the reality of Black and Brown communities.</p><p>We must ask ourselves: Will we face the truth of our past to build a more just future, or will we put on rose-colored glasses to avoid discomfort?</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-410000" name="module-410000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>The response to Floyd’s murder led corporations and organizations to <a class="Link" href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/shaunharper/2022/10/17/where-is-the-200-billion-companies-promised-after-george-floyds-murder/" target="_blank" >pledge more than $200 billion</a> toward racial equity, diversity initiatives and investments in historically disinvested communities of color. Schools made a promise to overhaul curricula and <a class="Link" href="https://www.edweek.org/leadership/defunded-removed-and-put-in-check-school-police-a-year-after-george-floyd/2021/06" target="_blank" >remove school resource officers</a>. Philanthropy made funding <a class="Link" href="https://racialequity.org/2024/05/4years-after-george-floyd/" target="_blank" >commitments of $16.5 billion</a> in 2020 for racial equity grants.</p><p>Yet, these public statements and promises did not endure. This racial reckoning also sparked discomfort that has evolved into powerful and organized cultural, systemic and legal backlash. </p><p>We have seen it in the <a class="Link" href="https://news.wttw.com/2025/05/22/despite-promises-promote-racial-equity-after-george-floyd-murder-many-companies-now" target="_blank" >rollback</a> of diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.prrac.org/censored-erased-and-whitewashed-jim-crow-education-in-the-twenty-first-century-january-april-2024-p-r-article/" target="_blank" >censorship</a> of our nation’s history in public school classrooms and the <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/news/2025/12/09/justice-department-discrimination-disparate-impact-00683362" target="_blank" >dismantling of protections</a> designed to address racial inequities. </p><p>For some, confronting the truth about our nation’s history — from slavery, segregation, exploited labor and ongoing inequities — proved easier in theory than in sustained practice.</p><p>This retreat is also clear in decisions like the recent U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Louisiana v. Callais<i> </i>that <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/04/29/nx-s1-5754657/supreme-court-louisiana-redistricting" target="_blank" >gutted the federal Voting Rights Act,</a><i> </i>signaling a broader erosion of civil rights safeguards that generations fought hard to secure. </p><p>In its decision, the court severely limited Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, making it much harder for Black, Latinos and other communities of color to challenge racial discrimination in voting — essentially arguing that racial discrimination is something of the past, rendering this protection unnecessary. </p><p>The court’s decision threatens to further divide our nation and entrench power in the hands of the few. Simply put, it jeopardizes our multiracial democracy.</p><p>To suggest that America is no longer shaped by its history is to ignore the very systems that continue to produce inequitable outcomes today. </p><p>Chicago is a clear example — it remains one of the most <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/race-class-communities/2023/06/19/chicago-remains-the-most-segregated-big-city-in-america" target="_blank" >segregated large cities</a> in the U.S. today. This is not by accident but rather systemically created by decades of discriminatory housing policies, inequitable public education and historical economic disinvestment in communities of color. </p><p>We cannot, in good faith, move forward with policy without considering the truth of our past that continues to shape our communities today.</p><p>We see this in our work every day at the Chicago Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights and the impacted communities with which we collaborate. Racial injustice permeates every system in our society, and communities of color continue to be barred from power and opportunity. To unpack centuries of systemic racism and build a more equitable society, we must pay attention for more than a moment.</p><p>Justice is not achieved through selective moments of outrage, but through sustained advocacy, policy reform, civic engagement and long-term commitments to this challenging work of fighting for racial justice. </p><p>It requires bravery from corporations and institutions when it becomes politically and culturally unpopular. It requires all of us to reject the false narratives that suggest equity efforts are divisive, unnecessary or unfair. It requires us to be honest about our nation's history, even when it’s uncomfortable.</p><p>Collectively, we must resist the temptation to treat racial justice as a passing political moment — the fight for racial equity did not start with George Floyd’s murder, and together, we can make sure it doesn’t end there.</p><p><i>Zindy Marquez is the director of communications at Chicago Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e40000" name="module-e40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Comedy clubs offer safe spaces for thoughtful inquiry on Iran war, current affairs
entries.summary: <p>A few weekends ago, I went to see Sammy Obeid at the <a class="Link" href="https://www.laughfactory.com/" target="_blank" >Laugh Factory</a> for a packed Sunday afternoon show. Sammy is a <a class="Link" href="https://sammyko.com/pages/about-us?srsltid=AfmBOopOBUGX-BSGm82IAqf4p3AKJYeAXyyscMz5sl1R2mjNhp438Dd_" target="_blank" >Lebanese, Palestinian, Syrian and Italian</a> American comedian, known for political comedy and math jokes. I’ve been following and admiring his work for some time.</p><p>I’m an Iranian American professor at Northwestern University by day and a burgeoning comic by night. As universities and public institutions face growing pressures around speech, dissent and intellectual freedom, I’ve come to see Chicago’s comedy scene as one of the few remaining spaces for open and radical inquiry. </p><p>Comedy, at its best, functions as both joy and rebellion in times of authoritarianism.</p><p>Sammy’s visit to the Laugh Factory came during the ongoing war on Iran, a subject that has consumed many Iranian Americans emotionally and spiritually for months. As I suspected, Sammy didn’t pull any punches. He was sharp, fearless and relentless in his criticisms of the war, calling out what he saw as the absurdity and arrogance of yet another U.S.-Israeli act of aggression in the Middle East.</p><p>In comedy parlance, he murdered. Unfortunately, so does the Islamic Republic in Iran, which Sammy largely left untouched in his set. His jokes fell short of clearly naming what many Iranians experience as the primary source of their suffering. </p><p>L.A.-based Iranian American comedian <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/hormozcomedy/" target="_blank" >Hormoz Rashidi</a> captures this tension in one of his recent bits, comparing the idea of Israel “saving” Iran to a parent asking Jeffrey Epstein to save their child. Both options are grotesque. But when conditions become unbearable, people begin considering the unthinkable.</p><p>Part of me wanted Sammy to hold more of that complexity, or at least to direct some of his comedic fire toward Iran's regime alongside Israel and the United States. He didn’t. And that’s perfectly OK. I still tip my hat to him. The work of the comedian, like the work of the artist and the scholar, is to make the hidden visible. To challenge all forms of power, especially the ones that are most uncomfortable to name.</p><p>As Chicagoans continue trying to make sense of the Iran conflict, I encourage people to support live comedy, especially Chicago’s local Iranian comedians. And there are many: <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/paulfarahvar/" target="_blank" >Paul Farahvar</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/sohrabisbrown/" target="_blank" >Sohrab Forouzesh</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/chrisbadercomedy/" target="_blank" >Chris Bader</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/mehdiamanicomedy/" target="_blank" >Mehdi Amani</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/milomackcomedy/" target="_blank" >Milo Mack</a> and others, including myself. I’m out there working through these ideas on stage as much as I am writing about them.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://sesp.northwestern.edu/people/faculty/sepehr-vakil.html" target="_blank" ><i>Sepehr Vakil</i></a><i>, associate professor, Northwestern University School of Education and Social Policy</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6f0000" name="module-6f0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Mosque shooting reminder of youth-related gun violence </h3><p>Two teenagers, ages <a class="Link" href="https://abc7.com/post/islamic-center-san-diego-shooting-teenage-suspects-identified-cain-clark-caleb-vazquez/19130299/" target="_blank" >17 and 18</a>, attacked a San Diego mosque Monday, <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/05/20/nx-s1-5827053/san-diego-mosque-shooting-victims" target="_blank" >killing three people</a>. After fatally shooting the victims — Mansour Kaziha, Amin Abdullah and Nadir Awad — the teen killed themselves. These male teens reportedly wore <a class="Link" href="https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-05-18/san-diego-islamic-center-shooting-suspects-what-we-know" target="_blank" >body armor</a> and were armed with handguns and rifles. After searching the homes where the teens lived with their families, authorities recovered more than <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/may/19/san-diego-mosque-shooting" target="_blank" >30 guns</a>.</p><p>In many of the articles about this horrific incident, these teens are referred to as “gunmen.” But that term doesn’t seem to fit these youth.</p><p>It’s time for the media and others to come up with a more accurate term to describe the children and older teens who get access to guns and commit violence. After all, we were forced to come up with the term "school shooter."</p><p>In thinking about what this new term should be, it’s good to remember that, thanks to the Republicans, the gun industry and the corrupt GOP Supreme Court, guns are the l<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/10/17/23919379/deaths-children-teens-leading-cause-firearms-homicide-suicide-prevention-the-conversation" >eading cause of death</a> for children in America.</p><p>Past estimates that <a class="Link" href="https://ojjdp.ojp.gov/model-programs-guide/literature-reviews/gun-violence-and-youth-young-adults#0-0" target="_blank" >more than 5,000 youths</a> — ages 12-24 — commit homicides with firearms every year and more than 3,400 young people — ages 10-24 — <a class="Link" href="https://everytownresearch.org/report/the-rise-of-firearm-suicide-among-young-americans/" target="_blank" >die by suicide</a> using a gun. So, young children/youth and guns are definitely a thing in our America.</p><p>So maybe the term "gunchild" should be used to describe the youngest perpetrators. The Republicans and the gun industry would probably love this new term. They could run booster programs for expanding the number of gunchildren across the country. Eventually, Republicans can pass laws, giving every child born in America his or her very first gun. Of course, these days, Republicans would only want that perk for newborns who are white.</p><p><i>Barry Owen, Lake View</i></p><h3>Make CTA’s acting president permanent leader </h3><p>In a world filled with horrible leaders, the CTA's Acting President <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/07/30/interim-cta-president-nora-leerhsen-permanent-post-dorval-carter" >Nora Leerhsen</a> is a welcome exception. </p><p>Since she replaced Dorval Carter Jr. over a year ago, she has proven to be the type of person you want running the Chicago Transit Authority. She rides the system. She takes her kids on the CTA. She visits workers in the field. Every CTA employee I have talked to has had something good to say.</p><p>She navigated the CTA through the fiscal cliff, federal budget cuts and oversaw the start of the Red Line extension. She’s increased communications and transparency and passionately believes that fast, frequent, reliable and safe transit benefits Chicago area residents, even those who don’t take the bus or train.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson — with weeks left before he has no say in who heads the transit agency — now wants to weigh and is pressing the CTA board to select a permanent president. </p><p>Chicagoans should remember Johnson’s transit judgment in 2024, when he nominated the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2024/05/24/mayor-brandon-johnson-ira-acree-regional-transportation-authority-board-nomination-withdrawal" >Rev. Ira Acree</a> to the Regional Transportation Authority board. Acree, pastor of the West Side's Greater St. John Bible Church, withdrew his nomination after saying <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2024/05/08/pastors-appointment-to-transit-board-advances-despite-saying-he-rarely-rides-cta/" target="_blank" >asinine things like</a>, “as a man, I don’t have to use CTA. I’m fortunate to have a car."</p><p>That is exactly the type of person we do not need in charge. We have a president in Washington who says things like that.</p><p>Leerhsen's only fault is that she’s not buddies with the mayor. But transit riders don’t care whether the person fixing bus service checks the right political box. They care whether the bus comes.</p><p>The infusion of new funding from last year’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/11/06/illinois-transit-spending-bill-tax-riders-drivers" >historic transit bill</a> has given us the opportunity to drastically improve CTA service and safety. If that money is used well — with a real transit nerd at the helm — this will directly result in fewer cars on the road, less traffic, cleaner air and a stronger economy. </p><p>The last thing Chicago needs now is some politically connected placeholder who’s just there for the paycheck. We need someone who sees public transit as a public good. Make Nora Leerhsen the permanent president.</p><p><i>Cyrus Dowlatshahi, Bucktown</i></p><h3>America: For the people? Or just the filthy rich?</h3><p>Is our federal government still truly of, by, and for the people? Or is it for Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg? Is our economic policy focused on supporting and maintaining financial fairness for a vigorous middle class, or does it exist to turn billionaires into trillionaires? </p><p>One need only look at the moneyed class President Donald Trump rubs elbows with to know the answer. </p><p>Who was by his side at his 2024 inauguration? The very, very richest Americans, while experienced diplomats, governors, members of Congress and many other life-long public servants were conspicuously seated in a separate area, with a closed-circuit television. </p><p>And who did <a class="Link" href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/5/14/who-are-the-us-ceos-in-china-with-trump-and-whats-in-it-for-them" target="_blank" >Trump take with him to China</a> on a long, cozy Air Force One flight? Again, the same people now so conveniently poised to enrich themselves and the first family. It almost makes Jimmy Carter's presidency look tragically naive as he took great care to isolate his modest <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2023/02/24/fact-check-jimmy-carter-put-peanut-farm-blind-trust-during-term-president/11340029002/" target="_blank" >peanut farm in a blind trust</a>, so as to avoid any appearance of enriching himself from his policies.</p><p>To be clear, being rich is not a crime. It is a feature of the motivation inherent in our historically successful capitalist society. Most Americans would love to be financially safe and secure, by dint of hard work and persistence. However, we desperately need federal leadership to understand the increasing pressures on poor and middle-class families, and to legislate accordingly.</p><p>Many people are rightfully frightened about their financial futures — not just for the years ahead, but for next week's groceries and next month's mortgage. </p><p>Millions of Americans wanted a businessman president and voted accordingly. But government is not a business. Financial wisdom and prudence are quality traits and motives. But while capitalism has proven to be a beneficial system, "cowboy" and predatory capitalism" are not. </p><p>Government is not a toy for wealthy people vying for the biggest yacht. It is a public calling of dedicated service to citizens, requiring specific mindsets and expertise. </p><p>Americans need that kind of vision in our governmental infrastructure and organization. We need a reset. Especially in this semiquincentennial year. "Of, by, and for the people" must be the defining mission statement of our democracy, not merely a relic of our 250-year history.</p><p><i>Jane Artabasy, Glencoe</i></p><h3>Trump’s unjust rewards </h3><p>President Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cvgzr7vr203o" target="_blank" >settled his $10 million lawsuit </a>against the Internal Revenue Service in exchange for a nearly <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/trump-doj-fund-irs-trump-family-lawsuit-c9aaa94c59988508c253d7200043cecc" target="_blank" >$1.8 billion fund</a> to reward insurrectionists who stormed the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. Will his generosity extend to the more than <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/a-difficult-year-how-officers-who-defended-the-capitol-are-grappling-with-efforts-to-downplay-jan-6-violence" target="_blank" >140 police officers</a> who were injured by those "patriots"? Will he grant compensation to the families of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us/officer-who-responded-us-capitol-attack-is-third-die-by-suicide-2021-08-02/" target="_blank" >four officers who died by suicide</a> due to the post-traumatic stress disorder they suffered from the events on Jan. 6? Or does Trump’s largesse only extend to criminals?</p><p><i>Paul L. Newman, Merion Station, Pennsylvania</i></p><h3>Toast for unionizing nurses</h3><p>Yes, I'm a guy who enjoys a good party. I'm also a guy who's been a patient at Rush University Medical Center. So, I was doubly interested to read the article by the Sun-Times' Elvia Malagón on the successful effort of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/05/18/rush-nurses-unionize-celebrate-vote" >Rush nurses to form a union</a>. </p><p>I've seen firsthand the expertise, diligence, and just plain human kindness that the nurses exhibit every day. I hope that this union will result in even better care for patients and just compensation for the nurses.</p><p>Oh, yeah, I liked that the article pointed out that the nurses gathered at the West Loop's Billy Goat Tavern to watch the union votes and passed around shots of Malort when victory was assured. The only downside to the celebration is that I didn't happen to wander into the Billy Goat while the nurses were there. </p><p>Congratulations, nurses! I'll raise a glass to your victory — though not with Malort — in absentia.</p><p><i>Jim Bruton, Avondale</i></p><h3>Replacing Mussolini’s gift</h3><p>Our city should replace the Balbo <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-history/2026/05/13/the-balbo-monument-is-in-rough-shape-what-should-we-do-with-it" target="_blank" >Monument</a> given by fascist Benito Mussolini with a statue of a more deserving Italian or Italian American.</p><p>Some candidates to consider: Dante Alighieri; St. Francis of Assisi; Mother Frances Xavier Cabrini.; Enrico Fermi; Galileo Galilei; Luigi Galvani; Giuseppe Garibaldi; Antonio Gramsci; Fiorello La Guardia; Rita Levi-Montalcini; Salvador Luria; Giuseppe Verdi and Alessandro Volta.</p><p>Several of these people were persecuted by Mussolini's fascist regime.</p><p><i>A. Christopher Wilson, West Rogers Park</i></p><h3>Out-of-state Bears can’t keep Chicago name </h3><p>If the Bears decide to play their home games in Indiana, the city of Chicago and the state of Illinois should request they drop "Chicago" from their name.</p><p>If they think Indiana is better for them, then don't use Chicago in their name.</p><p><i>Warren Rodgers Jr., Orland Park</i></p><h3>Beef with state leaders</h3><p>It's so nice to see our Illinois General Assembly hard at work passing legislation making the Italian beef our official state sandwich. I guess we have nothing more important to consider. Our tax dollars hard at work.</p><p><i>John Farrell,  DeKalb</i> </p><h3>For Pete’s sake </h3><p>If all that female White Sox fan said was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/19/pete-crow-armstrong-provides-context-about-viral-fan-interaction" target="_blank" >“you suck,”</a> then Pete Crow-Armstrong is every bit of the overrated player I think he is.</p><p><i>Jim Lanham, Joliet</i> </p><h3>Apology from Sox fans </h3><p>Dear Pete Crow-Armstrong,</p><p>We're sorry.</p><p>Signed, Real Sox fans</p><p><i>Pete Null, Glendale Heights</i><br></p>

entries.title: Honoring Sgt. Freddy Gonzalez and Latino valor on Memorial Day
entries.summary: <p>While the Trump administration is actively trying to rewrite American history, this Memorial Day would be a good time to remember and honor the sacrifices of the tens of thousands of Hispanic Americans who have served in our country’s wars. </p><p>Sixty have been awarded<i> </i>the Congressional Medal of Honor, according to the Congressional Medal of Honor Society. Here is the story of one of these brave Americans.</p><p>Alfredo “Freddy” Gonzalez grew up in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas. In the summers, he helped his family <a class="Link" href="https://vimeo.com/845308064" target="_blank" >pick cotton</a>. </p><p>Freddy was small in size, weighing 135 pounds, but he earned all-district honors in football, according to his U.S. Navy Memorial <a class="Link" href="https://navylog.navymemorial.org/gonzalez-alfredo" target="_blank" >biography</a>. He played hard. He played to win.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-950000" name="module-950000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>After graduating from high school, Freddy enlisted in the Marine Corps. The Marines sent him to Vietnam, and there he proved to be an excellent squad leader. Once his tour of duty ended and he came back to the States, the Marines made him an instructor.</p><p>Interviews conducted with family, friends and fellow Marines for a <a class="Link" href="https://vimeo.com/845308064" target="_blank" >historical video</a> produced for the Medal of Honor Society, along with other biographical information and a book about his life, tell the rest of the story: He had been stateside only a few months when he heard the bad news. There had been an ambush in 'Nam. Many of the men who had served under him were dead.</p><p>Freddy took it hard. He should have been there. They were his men. If he had been there, maybe they wouldn’t have been killed. What would a leader do? Would that person stay safe in the States while his fellow Marines were being killed? A leader would go back. He was going back. </p><h3>Commanding a platoon</h3><p>He was in 'Nam again and became a sergeant, but many things had changed. For one, he soon found himself in charge of a platoon. </p><h3></h3><p>Normally, a 48-man Marine platoon was commanded by a lieutenant, but many of the officers had either been killed or wounded, forcing Freddy to take command. For another, the men in his platoon had arrived in 'Nam only a few months before, according to the book "Marine Sergeant Freddy Gonzalez, Vietnam War Hero" by John W. Flores. He would have to train them, and before that, find some way to protect them. </p><p>Freddy’s good plans were literally blown to pieces when the Communists broke a ceasefire and invaded the old imperial city of Hue.</p><p>Freddy and his platoon were rushing down the road to protect Hue City when the cry was heard, the book says. “Ambush. Take cover.” A Marine riding on top of a tank was hit. He fell and lay bleeding in the road. </p><p>Immediately, Freddy left his position, ran to the man, picked him up, and carried him to safety, a Medal of Honor citation says. Freddy had been wounded. Looking over Freddy’s wounds, a medic wanted to evacuate him, but Freddy said no, the author, Flores, wrote in his book. He was not going to leave his men.</p><p>The last battle for Freddy and his men was in the abandoned <a class="Link" href="https://www.usmcmuseum.com/uploads/6/0/3/6/60364049/alfredo_gonzalez.pdf" target="_blank" >St. Joan d’Arc</a> Catholic Church and School in Hue. The fighting was brutal. Freddy’s platoon was being hit hard on all sides. Pinned down, his men were facing annihilation.</p><p>Then Freddy had a sudden idea. Why not blast the enemy with light anti-tank weapon rockets? Climbing the stairway of the church school, he ran through an open schoolroom door and fired all his rockets, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.military.com/history/marines-heroic-sacrifice-during-tet-offensive.html" target="_blank" >Military.com</a>. </p><p>This suppressed the enemy’s fire long enough to save his platoon from destruction. Then Freddy was hit by a sudden burst of return fire. He lay on the floor badly wounded. A Navy Corpsman arrived on scene and tried his best to save him, but the wound proved mortal. He died Feb. 4, 1968.</p><h3>‘Above and beyond call of duty’</h3><p>His citation says Marine Sgt. Alfredo Cantu Gonzalez was awarded the Congressional Medal of Honor "for conspicuous gallantry and intrepidity at the risk of his life above and beyond the call of duty while serving as platoon commander, 3d Platoon, Company A. … during the initial phase of Operation Hue City.” </p><p>Usually, that would be the end of the story. Freddy would be forever remembered by his family, his friends and the town he grew up in, but then the U.S. Navy stepped in. </p><p>In the mid-1990s, Navy officials named one of their newest guided-missile destroyers the USS Gonzalez (DDG-66). At the launching, Dolia Gonzalez, the single mother who had worked so hard to raise her only son and who had done so well, was there to christen the ship and see it off in 1995. </p><p>So, Freddy is on duty again, doing what he has always done — on patrol, keeping his family, his friends, his town and all of the rest of us safe from harm.</p><p>Protecting America.</p><p><i>William Dodd Brown is a lifelong Chicagoan and Vietnam-era veteran who publishes </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.weareallamericanpeople.com/" target="_blank" ><i>WeAreAllAmericanPeople.com</i></a><i>, a website that honors the achievements of Americans.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d40000" name="module-d40000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Delightful friend's 'wonderful' pup is no longer welcome
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> A friend of mine calls first or pops by every few months. She's generous and brings homemade treats, something she has found at the grocer's or flowers from her garden. We have great chats, and I really like her. The problem is, she always brings her little dog, whom she calls the most "wonderful little doggie in the world." He goes into all the rooms and jumps on the beds, couch, needlepoint chairs, etc. The last time she was here, I had to launder two bedspreads and clean the couch because it was muddy outside. When I spoke up and said maybe his feet were muddy, she said she had wiped his feet. Obviously not. I don't want her dog here anymore. I have a patio where we can visit, and I can direct her and the dog there when the weather is good, but what do I say in the meantime when she appears at my door with her dog? — <i>DISGRUNTLED IN MICHIGAN</i></p><p><b>DEAR DISGRUNTLED:</b> Direct her and her dog straight to the kitchen, close the door so her "wonderful" dog can't roam all over your house, and visit with them in there. It will make it more convenient for you both to eat her treats or arrange her flowers. If she asks you why, tell her that you love her little pooch, but you no longer want him on your furniture. You are within your rights to do that. If she becomes offended, it may end the friendship, but if you can't draw the line, your relationship will become increasingly less appealing anyway.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My younger sister, who is divorced, has raised two sons who are now young adults but strangers to me. Sis and I have had an on-and-off relationship, but we love each other regardless of our differences. I married a Frenchman and have lived in France for the last 30 years. I haven't seen Sis in 10 years. She has never been to France to visit me with her boys, although I have offered to pay for part of their expenses. We talk regularly, and I share photos of our family often. I haven't seen a photo of her boys for 10 years. When I ask why, she laughs and says her boys dislike having their pictures taken. I find that difficult to accept. I find it hurtful and sad that she refuses to share any photos of my nephews with me. I'd like to go see her, but I'm afraid I won't feel welcomed because of this. I feel she has isolated herself and her sons from the rest of her family. What should I do? — <i>ISOLATED SISTER ABROAD</i></p><p><b>DEAR SISTER:</b> Inform your sister that, after 30 long years, you are booking a trip to the U.S. to reconnect with friends and family, and ask if she would have time to visit with you and your family. Her response will tell you everything you need to know. From my perspective, the trip would be good for you, and you could make it with or without her blessing.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>What teens need to know about sex, drugs, AIDS and getting along with peers and parents is in "What Every Teen Should Know." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Teen Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Diesel fuel prices squeezing truckers, farmers and companies but shoppers will also pay the price
entries.summary: <p>Ricardo Guerrero arrives in the Loop every day around 5:30 a.m. to run his three food trucks, all serving authentic Mexican food.</p><p>The Cicero resident has been in the food truck business for five years. But this year has been unexpectedly difficult.</p><p>The rising price of diesel fuel, and even gasoline, has forced Guerrero to spend hundreds of dollars more per week in order to continue serving tourists and Chicagoans outside The Art Institute of Chicago and Shedd Aquarium.</p><p>While most consumers can find ways to cut back on gas, it's harder to escape the impact of diesel's record-breaking prices because it shows up in other ways.</p><p>“People have been focusing on gas prices because that's what hits them [at the pump]. But diesel affects all of us as well because almost everything that you eat, drink, use in your daily life has been on a truck or a rail car at some point,” Dana Regan, vice president of business development at TranzAct Technologies, a transportation management company, said.</p><p>Diesel prices in Illinois and the Chicago area hit an all-time high less than three months after the U.S.-Israel war with Iran began in February.</p><p>The average cost of diesel in the Chicago metro area reached a record $6.30 a gallon on May 15. Illinois diesel prices also smashed through its record that day, hitting $6.14 a gallon, according GasBuddy.</p><p>The new highs toppled the last records from June 2022, a few months after Russia invaded Ukraine. At the time, the Chicago-area's diesel price was $5.89.</p><p>Nationally, the average diesel price on Thursday was $5.64 a gallon, 19 cents below the June 2022 record of $5.83.</p><h3>Blocking the Strait of Hormuz</h3><p>Fuel prices have been climbing following Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. Twenty percent of the world’s oil supply passes through the Strait, but Iran has essentially closed off access, with the average number of ships passing through daily dropping by 95%, according to the UN Conference on Trade and Development. </p><p>President Donald Trump said Thursday that he was against Iran's plan to charge fees for passage through the Strait. "We want it open. We want it free. We don't want tolls," he said to reporters at the White House. "It's an international waterway."</p><p>Trump on Monday had threatened further attacks on Iran’s capital but pulled back, saying it was at the request of Gulf allies. </p><p>The Strait’s closure has caused the largest disruption the oil industry has ever faced, according to Sam Ori, executive director of the University of Chicago’s Institute for Climate and Sustainable Growth.</p><p>Michael Mahler, chief operating officer of HMD Trucking in Chicago Ridge, said the company's bottom line has worsened because of higher diesel prices, but it's also motivated the company to move quicker on its long-term strategy.</p><p>"From a day-to-day operations standpoint, we are regularly analyzing routes to identify more affordable states for fueling along those routes, as well as eliminating or changing some routes altogether," Mahler said in a statement. "On a larger scale, the current and historical instability in fuel prices has significantly expedited our renewable energy strategy. We will aggressively add Tesla EV Semis later this year to better protect us from diesel fuel instability in the coming years."</p><p>The price of diesel in the Chicago metro area has increased by 71% year over year, according to GasBuddy. Last May, diesel was $3.63. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-ab0000" name="html-embed-module-ab0000"></a><div class="flourish-embed flourish-chart" data-src="visualisation/29063122"><script src="https://public.flourish.studio/resources/embed.js"></script><noscript><img src="https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/29063122/thumbnail" width="100%" alt="chart visualization" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>While the average gas price rose <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/economy/2026/04/30/chicago-gas-prices-up-iran-war-5-gallon" >higher than $5</a> for the first time since 2022, diesel prices will likely impact consumers and business owners the most, experts say.</p><p>Guerrero said he typically spends about $500 every five days to fill up his three food trucks — two run on gas and the third needs diesel. Now, it costs him over $800.</p><p>In brighter times, he had planned to add three more Caseras Sabor Real food trucks, “but I would sell those trucks just to reinvest back in the three I already have,” he said.</p><p>Guerrero, 54, has been building up his savings over the years, but now he fears he'll need to dip into the account to keep operations running.</p><h3>Diesel’s impact on consumer prices</h3><p>"Diesel is what really powers the U.S. economy. From trains to tractors and trucks, diesel is the fuel that brings everything. If you look around you, everything is in your office or in your home because of diesel,” Patrick De Haan, petroleum analyst at GasBuddy, said."Supply chains up and down are powered by diesel."</p><p>The transportation, shipping, farming and logistics industry run on diesel, and the jump in price will lead to more <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/economy/2026/04/29/powell-fed-reserve-chair-ends-legal-actions-trump-administration" >inflation</a> for consumers already struggling with the rising living costs, according to Rachel Bronson, senior fellow on energy and geopolitics at the Chicago Council on Global Affairs.</p><p>Guerrero is already feeling the impact. He’s paying about 35% more for the ingredients in his well-loved quesabirria, or birria tacos,<b> </b>and its smoothies. The price of meat and produce, like lettuce and tomatoes, have also increased. He's worked out a line of credit with some suppliers, which allows him to pay the following month.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Northwestern University, said. “It’s going to be affected either by higher fertilizer cost or lower [harvests] because of the fertilizer cost.”</p><p>Crude oil is commonly used in fertilizer. The Green Markets Weekly North America Fertilizer Price Index reported Wednesday that the cost of fertilizer increased 30% year over year. </p><p>An American Farm Bureau Federation survey in April among 5,700 farmers found that 48% in the Midwest reported the greatest difficulty in securing fertilizer. Meanwhile, other regions reported a much harder time finding enough fertilizer. The bureau also said farm diesel prices — "a major operating expense during spring planting" — have risen 46% since the end of February.</p><p>Bronson said the increases in fertilizer and transportation costs show up in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/02/13/grocery-prices-chicago-climbed-inflation-trump-cpi-food" >grocery aisles</a>.</p><p>She said oranges, for example, imported to the U.S. will cost more because of higher transportation costs. That will mean shoppers are going to be charged more for oranges down the line or it will lead stores to carry less oranges, she said.</p><p>The spike in transportation fuel acts as a hidden tax on delivered goods.<b> </b></p><h3>‘Did not budget’</h3><p>Transportation and logistics companies were not prepared for a strain like this, Regan said.</p><p>“The biggest thing is people did not budget [for] a significant increase in transportation costs,” she said. “They prepare their 2026 budgets in 2025, and I don't think anyone saw this coming. [Companies] have to pass the costs on downstream. It's going to eventually affect the consumer.”</p><p>Bronson said shipping, often the cheapest way to transport goods, is also an industry facing headwinds, with companies adding fuel surcharges. April 26 and runs through Jan. 27, 2027.</p><p>“Transportation costs have been increasing, and our competitors have reacted with a number of surcharges,” the Postal Service said in news release. “We have steadfastly avoided surcharges and this charge is less than one-third of what our competitors charge for fuel alone.”</p><p>FedEx has a 27.25% surcharge in place for ground, home delivery, international ground and pick up services. The surcharge rate is 25.2% higher than its rates before the war. And its rates are updated weekly according to national diesel fuel prices, FedEx said.</p><p>UPS told its customers that starting May 18, it was adding an extra 27.75% fee on top of typical shipping costs on domestic ground packages.</p><p>“We're feeling it in terms of price at the pump, but we're really feeling it in terms of inflationary pressure that this energy crisis is causing for the everyday American,” Bronson said. “It’s probably the greatest concern for our economy right now.”</p><p>If the Strait were to open, the inflationary impact won’t go away, and prices aren’t likely to drop soon, Bronson said.</p><p>She said the unpredictability of the situation paired with “very little visibility and transparency” from leaders creates an unstable market.</p><p>“Even if the Strait of Hormuz [is] open tomorrow, the infrastructure has been hit,” she said. “It takes time to put the energy back onto the market. ... entries.title: What should we do with the sunken Raber? Landmark home faces uncertain future
entries.summary: <p>The old John Raber House was landmarked in 1996 and not without good reason: The 156-year-old Washington Park neighborhood residence is a surviving example of the 19th century country estate homes that once occupied the mid-South Side.</p><p>Plus, the house was vacant, dilapidated and sitting in a corner of the neighborhood that had been eroded by demolition. So the city acquiring the building and protecting it from being wrecked were solid steps that would lead to the home's — and the area's — turnaround.</p><p>So it seemed then.</p><p>Thirty years later, the Raber House, 5760 S. Lafayette Ave., still sits weathered and empty. And it could remain that way for a while. The city has outlined no clear plans for the building.</p><p>"City planning efforts have explored the restoration and adaptive reuse of the Raber House and [the Department of Planning and Development] has entertained interest from outside parties," the city's planning agency said in a statement. "But no viable proposals have been submitted to date."</p><p>The Raber House deserves better, and so does the Washington Park neighborhood, where signs of a rebound include an arts corridor — albeit University of Chicago-led — on Garfield Boulevard west of King Drive, about a mile east of the Raber.</p><p>Closer still: The Sweet Water Foundation, led by the urban designer and 2019 MacArthur Foundation genius grant fellow Emmanuel Pratt, operates a nationally-recognized community-focused urban agriculture and arts practice on lots right next to the Raber.</p><p>The house should be a plus and not a pall for Washington Park. It's time for the city to take the lead in finding a new use for this landmark.</p><p>The Raber is a substantial-looking 1870 Italianate-styled home with two-story bay windows flanking the main entrance and topped by a cupola with a hipped roof. </p><p>The house looked as if it were straight out of a seaside New England town.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of the Chicago Department of Planning and Development</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>John Raber, a real estate developer, businessman and politician — this is Chicago, after all — built the home and surrounded it with six lush acres of land.</p><p>The property was so large its entrance was a full block to the east on what is now State Street.</p><p>In the 1874 book "Chicago and its Suburbs," author Everett Chamberlin said the Raber had "finely graveled walks and drives bordered with beautiful arbor vitae hedges. Miniature lakes filled with gold-fishes, and other pleasing features are to be met at every hand."</p><p>By the 1890s, the area — like much of Chicago — turned into a boom town with industry and workers. The Raber's large grounds were subdivided for new homes and streets, and the home became just another house in the block. It was converted into a six-flat in 1894.</p><p>When disinvestment in Washington Park began hitting hard, starting in the 1970s, scores of homes and buildings built in the neighborhood between the 1890s and 1930s started falling to demolition.</p><p>By the time the Raber was landmarked in the 1990s, it was surrounded by land once more.</p><p>There have been a few ideas proposed for the house. Back in 2011, the area's then-Ald. Willie Cochran wanted to turn the house and land into a vineyard.</p><p>The city owns 29 parcels of land around the house, a planning department spokesperson said. In another idea for the site, the nonprofit conservation group Openlands acquired four of those parcels on the city's behalf.</p><p>"It was to create a park around the Raber House and kind of bring it back to that pastoral original design that it had," Openlands Vice President of Policy and Land Conservation Emily Reusswig said.</p><p>But the idea went nowhere.</p><p>Some of the land is being used, however. Sweet Water owns or is activating at least four lots by the Raber. The organization's mix of art, education and urban agricultural is aimed at revitalizing communities without pushing out residents.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Lafayette Ave. in Englewood, Monday, May 11, 2026. | Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>I wanted to know what Pratt thought of what should happen with the Raber, but neither he nor a Sweet Water representative returned calls for this column.</p><p>Judging by the organization's website, they've given the building some serious thought.</p><p>"The Raber House offers a singular reductive and colonial historical narrative that lacks any connection to its present day context," the website says. "Yet, it has been highlighted as the one and only promise of utopian development, somehow capable of resurrecting a neighborhood that has otherwise been deemed undesirable and ill-suited to be amidst its glory."</p><p>Strong words. But correct ones. </p><p>The Raber's value isn't in what it was then, but in what it must become now, in order to serve the folks of Washington Park and the South Side. That means the city and stakeholders must work together to investigate and unlock potential new uses for the Raber.</p><p>Hard work, yes. But it's better than city government just waiting around for a developer to serve up a deal that could be years away and no doubt require taxpayer subsidy — as is too common a practice in this town.</p><p>To its credit, the city has done some minor work on the Raber over the past decade to keep the house somewhat weathertight, so it doesn't wind up falling in on itself.</p><p>But the house won't be truly saved until it's restored and operational.</p>

entries.title: How we photographed one of two million Americans living with limb loss
entries.summary: <p>This week’s top photo comes from Visual Journalist <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/authors/anthony-vazquez" target="_blank" >Anthony Vazquez</a>. Follow him on <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/avazquezphoto?utm_source=ig_web_button_share_sheet&igsh=ZDNlZDc0MzIxNw==" target="_blank" >Instagram</a>.</p><h3>What makes this photo important?</h3><p>Amputees and individuals with disabilities are often underrepresented in general news coverage. L. Bradley Schwartz, who underwent 24 different amputations after he got sick with meningococcal meningitis, is a lawyer and a peer mentor at Shirley Ryan AbilityLab for people who have undergone amputations. Sharing Schwartz's story honors his personal journey through tragedy and shows how got through it. Ultimately, stories and images like this allow others going through similar situations to see themselves reflected in the news, offer comfort and potentially encourage them to reach out to advocacy groups or support networks.</p><h3>How did you get the photo?</h3><p>When I arrived, the office was lit by harsh overhead fluorescent lighting and filled with busy posters and personal items. I decided to turn off the overhead lights and rely entirely on the natural light from a single window. While a window-lit portrait is a common technique, it was necessary here to naturally separate Bradley from the background clutter without using an artificial flash. By letting the rest of the office fall into shadow, the distractions disappear, drawing all attention directly to Bradley. This choice was deliberate: I wanted the viewer to focus on him as a person and look toward his future, rather than just focusing on his disabilities.</p><p><b>Technical details</b><br></p><ul
